newsitem.title: USA: Oil majors seen strong gasoline buyers in US Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Oil majors seen strong gasoline buyers in US Gulf.

text.p: U.S. Gulf Coast players were bracing themselves Thursday for new animated buying of conventional unleaded gasoline, with Exxon and other majors expected to snap up barrels of the suddenly scarce commodity.

Differentials firmed 2.5 cents a gallon Wednesday on a gumbo of bullish factors, including lower production aggravated by refinery problems at Petroleos de Venezuela's Amuay refinery and Amoco's huge Texas City, Texas refinery.

Prompt 31st cycle Gulf parcels traded Wednesday for 3.75 cents over December futures but eased down a bit to 3.0 cents over late in the day, traders said. That compares with only 0.40 cent over the print on Tuesday.
"Exxon is buying about 75,000 to 100,000 more barrels than normal today; they're not usually this net short," one Gulf trader said Thursday morning.
Other players said Exxon bought substantial parcels Wednesday, but could not yet confirm a repeat of the same big volumes today.
Amoco and Citgo, the U.S. unit of PDVSA, were also seen yesterday as big takers of M4, traders said.
Amoco notified regulators on Monday of problems with a fluid catalytic cracker at its 433,000 barrel per day refinery in Texas City.
PDVSA is making repairs to a downed cat cracker at its 510,000 bpd Amuay refinery expected to take until mid-November.
One Gulf trader said he expected sellers to hold out this morning, pushing M4 back to yesterday's highs. "But prices could come back down a bit by late afternoon," he added.
The Gulf Coast's Refinery Row has been cutting back on gasoline production in the past six weeks in order to maximize distillate production to fill the gap in U.S. stocks ahead of winter.
Gasoline production has begun to ramp back up, however, with API data showing production jumping to 7.62 million barrels per day for the week ending Oct 25 -- 363,000 bpd more than the prior week.
But traders said it could take a while for the newly increased production to ease the current tightness in supply.
